title: Exposure and dynamic range — Image Wiki
text:
Exposure and dynamic range
  How much light got recorded, and how far apart the brightest and darkest thing can be before one of them stops recording at all.

  
    Termexposure / dynamic range
    Also calledblown highlights, clipping, crushed blacks, exposure triangle, tonal range
    Not the same ascontrast, brightness, the HDR look, white balance
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Exposure: three controls, three pricesDynamic range: why the window goes whiteClipping is not the same as darkWhat a histogram tells you and what it does notYour eye is not a better sensor
      
    
  

  Stand in a room with a window on a bright day and take one photo. Standing there, your eyes had no trouble seeing both the room and the view. The camera has to pick.


Exposed for the view out of the window
Exposed for the room, several stops brighter


Axel Jacobs, 2006, two frames from one bracketed set: same room, same window, same time of day, only the exposure changed. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.
Left: the view records properly — separate leaves, power lines against blue sky, an iron fence, coloured marbles on the sill. Indoors is gone: the dressmaker's dummy is a flat silhouette, the armchair a shape you could not identify.
Right: the room records properly — cream walls, dado rail, floorboards, a red chair with a yellow cushion. Now look back at the window: one flat white panel with a ghost of foliage low in the glass. The power lines, the sky and the fence are not in the file.


Two separate things are going on. Exposure is how much light the camera collected. Dynamic range is how far apart the brightest and darkest thing can be while both still record with detail. Exposure is a choice; dynamic range is a hard limit of the medium, and the world routinely exceeds it.
Exposure: three controls, three prices



Control
What it does
What it costs




Aperture, f/1.4 to f/22
Sets the area light passes through. f/1.4 admits about 256 times as much light as f/22
Depth of field — wide open, only a thin slice is sharp


Shutter, 30 s to 1/4000 s
Sets how long light is collected. Double the time, double the light
Motion blur and camera shake, or frozen motion you did not want


ISO, 100 to 25600
Amplifies whatever was collected
Noise. Grain in the shadows, mush in fine detail



Many combinations give the same brightness. f/8 at 1/60 and f/4 at 1/250 record the same light and make very different photographs. A landscape sharp from foreground rock to horizon and with silky water is a small aperture forcing a long shutter, on a tripod, both effects arriving together. Reading those trade-offs backwards out of a picture is most of what guessing how it was shot amounts to, alongside the camera position you can read off the perspective (Focal length vs camera position).
Dynamic range: why the window goes white
Think of each pixel on a sensor as a bucket collecting photons. Fill the bucket and it saturates: every extra photon is invisible, and that is the top of the range. The bottom is not zero either, because the electronics have their own noise floor, and once the signal is quieter than the noise there is nothing left to read. Dynamic range is the gap between those two.
It is counted in stops, where one stop is a doubling. Ten stops means the brightest recordable thing is 1024 times the darkest. In practice a digital camera gives you 8 to 12 stops, more at low ISO, and more from a large sensor with big pixels.
Now the scenes. A flat overcast day with nothing dark in frame might span 3 stops, comfortably inside the camera. A sunny day with black rock, white foam and a glint off a car runs to 12 stops or beyond. The room above is worse than either.
The chain has more links after the sensor. Print is far worse: paper cannot be brighter than white paper under the light in the room, and its black is limited by pigment. Screens do better, but only in the dark.
Clipping is not the same as dark
Clipped means the data is gone. Every pixel in that region sits at maximum (or minimum) with nothing between them. Nothing recovers it: no slider and no model can put back a texture that was never measured.



Daniel Schwen, 2003. The same frame twice: below, every pixel sitting at pure white has been repainted red. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5.
Look at the steel table plate across the bottom. Its left half is full of information — scratches, punch marks, a dent, the grain of the metal. Its right half, where the sun lands, is one continuous red field: same plate, same material, no surface recorded at all. In the upper picture that passes for an ordinary highlight on metal.
The daylight behind the men is solid red too, with no gradient in it. The pale jacket is stippled red across the shoulder — half the pixels at the limit, half just under — which is what a surface sitting right on the edge of the range looks like. Everything unmarked still holds tone, the near-black cast iron of the press included.


Dark by choice is a different animal. A low-key portrait can be mostly shadow and still show the shirt seam, the hair against the background, the wall behind. Film noir is built on exactly that: huge areas of near-black that still hold shape. Look for whether the dark region has steps in it.
Colour channels clip on their own too. A red flower in direct sun blows the red channel while green and blue stay fine, so the petals lose their veining and go to a flat block while the rest of the picture looks correctly exposed.
What a histogram tells you and what it does not
A histogram is a tally: sort every pixel by brightness and stack them up. Height is how many pixels sit at that brightness. Nothing cleverer than that.

0black255whitebrightness of a pixelScene inside the camera's rangeovercast street: darkest to brightest spans about 6 stops0black255whitebrightness of a pixelall darker pixels record as 0all brighter pixels record as 255Same scene, sun out, wider than the rangeabout 12 stops — the ends fall off both edges

The same distribution of tones twice, once inside the camera's range and once wider than it.
Left: the mass sits clear of both walls — what "nothing clipped" looks like. Right: the scene spans more stops than the sensor holds, so every pixel darker than the low limit records as 0 and every brighter one as 255, piling into a single bin at each end. The spikes run off the top of the box because far more pixels land there than at any ordinary brightness. A spike pinned against an extreme edge is the one thing a histogram tells you with certainty.


It answers two more questions well. How much contrast is there — a wide spread means big brightness differences, a narrow central hump a flat image. And where the mass sits: bunched right is high key, bunched left is low key.
It cannot tell you where in the frame those tones are, which is the whole of composition. It cannot tell you whether the exposure was right, either: a snow field should pile up on the right and a night street should pile up on the left. There is no correct histogram shape, and anyone insisting the hump belongs in the middle is describing an average grey scene.
One trap. Most cameras show an RGB histogram, which stacks the three channels without caring whether they came from the same pixel. Cambridge in Colour's example is a set of saturated colour patches containing no white pixels at all: the RGB histogram screams clipping, the luminance histogram shows nothing near full brightness. Both are right about different things, and the more saturated the colours the more they disagree.
Your eye is not a better sensor
The eye's advantage is not raw range in one glance. Estimates for the instantaneous range, pupil fixed and adapted to one part of a scene, land around 10 to 14 stops. Across a full sweep of adaptation, starlight to noon, it is nearly 24 stops — but that is not one look. What the eye does is adapt and process locally: you scan the room, pupil and retina adjust, and the brain assembles one impression out of many differently adapted glimpses. It also judges brightness relative to neighbours, so a white shirt in shadow still reads white even when it is physically darker than a grey wall in sun.
So perceived contrast is not the same as a medium's dynamic range. A print holding 6 or 7 stops can look convincing because the eye reads relationships. It is also why the over-processed HDR look fails: pulling every shadow and highlight toward the middle destroys those relationships, and the result reads flat while containing more information. Which parts should be dark is a question about Value structure, not about capture.

Clipped means gone
"I will fix the sky in post" only works if the sky was recorded. Check for a flat, single-valued white with no gradient before assuming anything is recoverable.


Reading exposure off an image

Find the brightest area. Any texture or gradient in it, or one flat value with a hard edge?
Find the darkest area. Can you separate two objects inside it?
If either is flat, ask whether the scene forced it. A window, a sun in frame or a lamp in a dark room usually did.
Check saturated colours separately. Red and blue clip before the picture as a whole looks bright.
Empty dark with a hard boundary is a capture failure; dark with structure in it is a decision. See Hard and soft light for what kind of light makes each likely.



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Depth of field
              The band of distance that comes out looking sharp. Everything outside it blurs, and how that blur grows tells you whether a picture came out of a real camera.
            
          
        
          
            
              Focal length vs camera position
              Where the camera stands decides how big near things look next to far things. The lens only decides how much of that view fits in the frame.
            
          
        
          
            
              Value structure
              How light or dark things are, independent of their colour. Squint at any image and what survives is its value structure — and if that does not read, no colour will save it.
            
          
        
          
            
              Hard and soft light
              Whether shadows have crisp edges or fade gradually. It is decided by one thing — how big the light looks from where the subject is standing.
